item.title: “Sunakkhatta, suppose there is a very poisonous viper. Then a man comes who desires to live, not to die, who desires happiness and loathes suffering.…
item.description:
“Sunakkhatta, suppose there is a very poisonous viper. Then a man comes who desires to live, not to die, who desires happiness and loathes suffering. What do you think, Sunakkhatta? Would that man give his hand or his foot to that viper if he knew: ‘If I am bitten by this snake, I will meet death or deadly suffering’?”
“No, venerable sir.”
“So too, Sunakkhatta, a monk should surely guard himself in regard to the six sense-bases. Knowing that ‘Attachment is the root of suffering,’ he becomes unattached and liberated by the destruction of attachment. It does not happen that he would still focus his body on attachment or direct his mind to attachment.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 105 – Sunakkhattasutta

item.title: “Monks, wander in your own proper range, in your own ancestral territory. Monks, if you wander in your own proper range, in your own ancestral…
item.description:
“Monks, wander in your own proper range, in your own ancestral territory. Monks, if you wander in your own proper range, in your own ancestral territory, then longevity will increase, beauty will increase, ease will increase, wealth will increase, power will increase.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 26 – Cakkavattisutta

item.title: “So too, venerable sirs, the eye is not the bondage of forms, nor are forms the bondage of the eye. Whatever desire and lust arises…
item.description:
“So too, venerable sirs, the eye is not the bondage of forms, nor are forms the bondage of the eye. Whatever desire and lust arises in dependence on both — that is the bondage there. The ear is not the bondage of sounds … The nose is not the bondage of odors … The tongue is not the bondage of tastes … The body is not the bondage of touches … The mind is not the bondage of phenomena, nor are phenomena the bondage of the mind. Whatever desire and lust arises in dependence on both — that is the bondage there.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 41.1

item.title: “Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? Form, monks, is…
item.description:
“Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? Form, monks, is not yours — abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. Feeling … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is not yours — abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.33

item.title: “Monks, what is clinging and worry? Here, monks, an untaught ordinary person, not seeing the noble ones, not skilled in the noble Dhamma, not trained…
item.description:
“Monks, what is clinging and worry? Here, monks, an untaught ordinary person, not seeing the noble ones, not skilled in the noble Dhamma, not trained in the noble Dhamma, not seeing the true persons, not skilled in the true Dhamma, not trained in the true Dhamma, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. For him, that form changes and alters. Because of the change and alteration of form, his consciousness follows that change in form. Worrying states arise from that consciousness following the change in form, invading his mind and remaining. Because his mind is invaded, he is terrified, distressed, and full of longing and worry.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.7

item.title: Elder Mahā-Moggallāna: With hut whose roof is made of bones, Sewn together with sinews and flesh — Foul, full of stench! Carrying other people’s limbs…
item.description:
Elder Mahā-Moggallāna:

With hut whose roof is made of bones,
Sewn together with sinews and flesh —
Foul, full of stench!
Carrying other people’s limbs
As my own body!

The container full of feces,
Covered over with skin —
O female demon!
With your breasts like boils —
Your body has nine streams,
Always flowing.

Your body’s nine streams,
Foul, creating bondage —
The monk avoids that body
As a clean person avoids feces.

If others knew you
As I know you,
They would avoid you
As one avoids feces in the rain.

It is truly so, O Great Hero,
As the ascetic said:
Here, some are stuck,
Like an old ox in the mud.

One who thinks he can dye
The sky with turmeric,
Or with any other color —
That one only fails.

My mind is like that sky —
Well concentrated internally —
Do not bring evil thoughts to it,
Like a bird falling into a pile of fire.

From: Theragāthā 20.1

item.title: One who does not lust for forms, Seeing a form, does not cling, His mind does not adhere to the feeling, He does not remain…
item.description:
One who does not lust for forms,
Seeing a form, does not cling,
His mind does not adhere to the feeling,
He does not remain attached to forms.
As he sees forms,
Feeling feelings accordingly,
It wanes away, not accumulated —
Thus mindful he practices.
Thus suffering is not stored up,
He is said to be close to Nibbāna.

One who does not lust for sounds,
Hearing a sound, does not cling …
One who does not lust for odors,
Smelling an odor, does not cling …
One who does not lust for tastes,
Tasting a flavor, does not cling …
One who does not lust for touches,
Feeling a touch, does not cling …

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.95

item.title: “What is the cause, good sirs, what is the condition for the non-arising of unarisen greed, or for the abandonment of arisen greed?” - “The…
item.description:
“What is the cause, good sirs, what is the condition for the non-arising of unarisen greed, or for the abandonment of arisen greed?” - “The sign of the foul.” For one who attends wisely to the sign of the foul, unarisen greed does not arise and arisen greed is abandoned. This, good sirs, is the cause, this is the condition for the non-arising of unarisen greed and for the abandonment of arisen greed.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.68

item.title: “Monks, I do not see any other class of things that is as diverse as the mind. Those beings in the animal realm — such…
item.description:
“Monks, I do not see any other class of things that is as diverse as the mind. Those beings in the animal realm — such beings are diverse because of their minds. Therefore, monks, one should constantly reflect on one’s own mind thus: ‘For a long time, this mind has been defiled by greed, hatred, and delusion. Through the defilement of the mind, beings are defiled. Through the purification of the mind, beings are purified.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.100

item.title: “Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye—these are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing.…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye—these are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. Sounds cognizable by the ear … Odors cognizable by the nose … Tastes cognizable by the tongue … Tangibles cognizable by the body—these are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta
